Acoustic parameter comfort of a classroom is impacted by multiple aspects that must not be disregarded. Although
Conceptual framework there have been several studies on classroom acoustics, there is a shortage of thorough reviews
that examine the impact of design factors in predicting acoustic quality. The aim of this study is to
develop a conceptual framework for classroom acoustic comfort that encompasses the objectives
of i) identifying various design enablers that may contribute to optimal acoustic comfort for
learning purposes and ii) analysing the influence of each design enabler on significant acoustic
parameters for classrooms. An analysis of 74 publications was carried out to examine the effects
of various classroom design factors on acoustic performance. The study identifies six design en-
ablers for classroom acoustic comfort: material, volume, layout, amplification system, noise, and
occupancy and five acoustic parameters: reverberation time, background noise, signal-to-noise
ratio, speech transmission index and speech clarity. A conceptual framework is proposed for
designers, researchers, and end-users to consider the enablers’ roles in creating an optimal
classroom learning environment.
1. Introduction
Teaching and learning activities are principally conducted in a learning space known as a classroom. The classroom plays an
important role in ensuring that learners receive knowledge content delivered by the teachers in a precise and distinctive way [1].
According to American Speech-Language-Hearing Association [2], and Rosenberg et al. [3], speaking and listening are the key means
of communication in the educational context where approximately 45–75 % of the student’s time is spent understanding the speech
from the teacher and peers in the classroom. Environmental elements such as lighting, thermal comfort, indoor air quality, and
acoustics have a great impact on the efficiency of learning processes in the classroom [4] and acoustics is categorised as one of the
enablers that influences a student’s learning achievement and the educator’s well-being the most [5]. According to Hamida et al. [6],
students’ acoustical preferences and needs are related to three indicators: occupant-related, dose-related, and building-related.

It is well established that adequate acoustical performance in school classrooms is required to encourage students’ interaction and
attention [7]. A favourable acoustic condition inside the classroom enables learners to concentrate more readily on their studies [8].
Poor acoustic conditions, such as prolonged exposure to loud noises and longer reverberation time [11,12], seriously harm non-lexical
activities such as memory, reading ability, attention, and motivation [9], as well as numeracy skills [10].
To ensure the comfort and effectiveness of teaching and learning in a classroom, good performance of acoustics conditions must be
considered. Several acoustic parameters require critical attention while designing a classroom. The four main prominent factors to be
acknowledged to achieve good acoustic performance for classroom design are Reverberation time (RT) [13], Background noise (BN)
[5], Speech Transmission Index (STI) [14], and Speech clarity (C50) [15]. Most developed nations have produced acoustic standard
guidelines for the school classroom. Reverberation time (RT) and background noise (BN) define classroom acoustic performance
criteria in the United States and the United Kingdom. According to a study by ANSI/ASA S12.60 [16], a classroom with ideal acoustic
conditions must meet the following criteria: background noise levels must not exceed 35 dB(A) in unoccupied conditions,
signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) ratio speech level over background noise must be +15 dB and above, and reverberation time must not
exceed 0.6 s and 0.7 s in small and large size classrooms. Meanwhile, based on established acoustic regulations for classrooms as stated
in Ref. [17], all school classrooms must adhere to certain conditions where the background noise must not exceed 35 dB and rever-
beration time must be less than 0.6 s for primary schools and 0.8 s for secondary schools respectively.
In most nations, the standard for classroom background noise levels has been established at 30–35 dB(A). However, each country’s
criteria for other acoustical factors vary significantly due to language differences. The acoustic requirements, particularly for rever-
beration time in countries such as Chile, Norway, and Denmark, are set at 0.6 s, and 0.8 s of reverberation time has been established for
Germany, France, Italy, and China [1]. In countries like South Africa and India, a standard guideline for classroom reverberation time
is yet to be established [18,19]. However, some nations’ acoustical requirements for classrooms have been developed as extensions of
general building acoustics rules or laws; however, in a recent trend that is still present today, many other nations are adjusting or
establishing requirements to meet the unique needs of children [20]. It has been discovered that the ability to interpret speech in noise
and reverberation is still growing at young ages (i.e., up to 11 years of age), and elementary school children may have a more difficult
time than older children in noisy and reverberant settings [21].
Regardless of differences in classroom acoustic regulation among the countries, the main objective derived from the established
guidelines is to optimise speech intelligibility (quality of speech transferred from speaker to listener) in the classroom. Speech
intelligibility (SI) is greatly affected by classroom acoustic parameters, namely reverberation time (RT), Background Noise Level
(BNL), Speech level (SL), Signal to Noise Ratio (SNR) and Useful-to-detrimental sound ratio values (U50). The Speech Transmission
Index (STI) and beneficial-to-harmful sound ratios (U50) are two objective methods to measure and predict speech intelligibility. U50
can be calculated by using C50 values and SNR [22]. It has been proven by Cho [23] that the combined impacts of room acoustics (C50)
and SNR values on speech intelligibility in classrooms may be measured by U50, which is nearly as accurate as STI values.
Despite the significant number of papers on the research subject, the literature lacks review, specifically on the role of classroom
design on acoustic performance and the relationship between the parameters involved. The rationale for this undertaking originated
from the necessity to address this gap, and it encompasses the subsequent objectives: i) to conduct a review on various design enablers
that contribute optimal acoustic comfort for occupants, and ii) to analyse the influence of each design enabler on significant acoustic
parameters for classrooms. While examining the present findings in light of the limitations identified in prior research, two (2) research
questions (RQ) were developed as follows:
RQ1: What design enablers must be considered in ensuring the acoustical performance of a classroom? This analysis aims to examine and
enumerate the various factors that contribute to the design of a classroom, which are essential for ensuring optimal acoustic
comfort for students.
RQ2: How do the acoustic parameters respond to different design enablers in a classroom? An analysis of the influence of each design
enabler on acoustic parameters in classrooms was performed. The result determines the important acoustic design enablers for
classrooms and their responses to each parameter. Based on this analysis, future suggestions are provided to identify viable ap-
proaches to achieving optimal acoustic comfort in the classroom.
2. Methods
2.1. Literature search
For the first research question, electronic databases Science Direct, Scopus, and Google Scholar were explored to gather an optimal
amount of quality, peer-reviewed research publications. This study conducted a systematic review to identify and evaluate relevant
scientific literature and analyse the present level of knowledge. The relationship between design enablers and overall acoustic comfort
in educational environments is constructed using systematic approaches to gather and combine the findings of past studies. A sys-
tematic literature review offers an in-depth review of the steps involved in scoping, planning, identifying, filtering, and including
relevant information. It also allows for repetition of the process to verify the findings and conclusions, shown in Fig. 1. This study
focused on classroom design enablers that determine the acoustic comfort of a classroom.
The review also encompasses the impact of design enablers on acoustic parameters, utilizing various methods such as in-field
observations, simulation measurements, and calculation prediction, to address the second research question. During the initial
stage of the literature search, a total of 1127 articles were acquired by using specific keywords such as classroom acoustics, acoustic
performance, acoustic conditions, and acoustic parameters, respectively. The article search was performed using online database
systems, specifically ScienceDirect, Scopus, and Google Scholar. These databases contain several multidisciplinary publications

The articles that were collected for the review were published from 1998 to 2023. The review process started in May 2023 and
concluded in mid-February 2024. Subsequently, the data analysis commenced after the data extraction was completed in mid-
December 2023. Table 1 highlights the review stages, with the keywords, search strings, inclusion criteria, and exclusion criteria
used in the study.
2.2. Selection and extraction of articles
As shown in Fig. 1, 1127 articles were acquired according to the keyword and search string presented in Table 1 to be filtered for
duplication in the identification stage. 301 articles were found to be duplicated according to the title, thus removed.
Next, the remaining 826 articles were screened to filter out 75 incomplete, non-English, and review articles. From the 75 articles
excluded in the first phase of screening, two (2) were incomplete, one (1) was non-English, and 72 were review articles. During the
second stage of the screening process, 751 articles were analysed based on the title, topic, and abstract screening. 432 articles were
identified as irrelevant to the present study due to a lack of accessibility of the full article. Articles that related to the effect of classroom
acoustics on the psychological and physiological health of the students were also regarded as irrelevant to the present study.
During the final stage (the third stage) of the screening process, the remaining 319 articles were analysed to align with the study’s
aim, methods, and outcomes. Several of the remaining articles were found to be unrelated; thus, only 74 scientific publications were
selected for further analysis using the PRISMA approach.
2.3. Data categorisation and extraction
The data categorisation and extraction used a matrix-structured approach to systematically arrange and examine the data. The data
categorisation was conducted in accordance with the aim and objectives of the present investigation. The elements comprising a matrix
approach are the title, authors, aim, methodologies, procedures, findings, and recommendations. The articles obtained from the
previous stage indicated that the methods employed were diverse and included in-field measurement, calculation prediction, and
simulation measurement. The data classification categorisations were determined based on the objectives, which include independent
variables (classroom design enablers) and dependent variables (acoustic characteristics and performance).
The data extraction process involves selectively filtering the raw data obtained from the matrix tables approach in order to conduct
targeted analysis that is in line with the study objectives. The raw data that has been extracted will be condensed to emphasise the main
discoveries of the current investigation. The data extraction summary encompasses the assessment of classroom design enablers and
their influence on the measured parameters.
2.4. Identification and evaluation (analysis stage)
The analysis phase took place once the data had been categorised and extracted. At first, the publication trends of the chosen
publications, comprising the year of publication and geographical distribution, were analysed to provide an overall understanding of
knowledge development in a particular discipline. Then, the analysis step involved the identification of design enablers, acoustic
parameter evaluation, and the influence of classroom design enablers on acoustic comforts. The data entry in matrix tables was filtered
based on the study’s focus on classroom design enablers. The filtered data was then classified into specific categories such as materials,
noise, volume, occupancy, amplification system, and layout.
The instrument for data collection is based on two variables: plausible classroom design enablers (the independent variable) and
acoustic performance (the dependent variable). Categorising these variables assisted the study in determining the appropriate design
enablers’ responses to acoustic performances. Three prominent categories of classroom design enablers are physical, human, and noise
attributes. Data from each category is further extracted to determine the subcategories and identify the acoustic performance impacted
by these subcategories. Ultimately, these data-driven findings were constructed to develop a conceptual framework for classroom
acoustic comfort. An important aspect is the development of a framework for classroom acoustic comfort, as it serves several purposes,
all of which promote the creation of an ideal learning environment while also recognising the educators’ wellbeing. Fig. 2 shows the
flowchart of analysis process for the present study.

3. Results and discussions
3.1. Overview of publication trends
The selected articles were initially analysed for publication trends to provide a view of how research output evolves over time and
across different regions, offering insights into the dynamics and global reach of scholarly activity within a specific discipline. Fig. 3
displays the chronological patterns of the current research topics chosen between 1995 and 2023, before the data extraction process
using the selection criteria. During the last two decades, research on the acoustic comfort of classrooms has experienced fluctuations,
reaching its highest number of studies in 2013, 2016, 2020, and 2021. All the filtered references specifically address the influence of
classroom design on acoustic quality. All the research involves on-site measurement, computer modelling, and calculated prediction.
As depicted in Fig. 4, the selected studies were predominantly and primarily conducted in Europe and Asia, making up 36 % and 35 %
of the literature, respectively. North America represents 10 % of the total, and South America represents 11 %. Only 8 % of the studies
originated in Australia, Algeria, Egypt, and Saudi Arabia.

3.3. Classroom acoustic parameters evaluation
Fig. 6 summarises previous studies’ findings on various classroom acoustic parameters through different methods, including field

3.4. Classroom acoustic design enablers influence on acoustic comfort
Various studies have investigated the quality of classroom acoustics in different countries. A classroom with ideal acoustic con-
ditions must incorporate several factors during the initial design and operation phase. Unlike in cinemas and concert halls, the
determining factors for achieving optimum acoustic comfort in a classroom differ where speech intelligibility is the main concern.
According to the present findings, six (6) enablers for classroom acoustic comfort have been identified: material, volume, layout,
amplification system, noise, and occupancy as shown in Fig. 7. All enablers were derived from in-depth analysis during the review
process, and the details of the findings are to be discussed further in this section. General information on references for each design
enabler review process is presented in Table 3.
3.4.1. Material
A practical selection of materials used in a classroom plays an important role in ensuring the optimisation of the acoustic condition.
Generally, classroom acoustic treatment by applying absorptive materials is required to establish lower reverberation time where
excessive sound reflection can be minimised [27,92]. As reported by Ref. [28], the main reason for higher reverberation time in a
classroom is due to unsuitable finishing materials used for floor and wall, an excessive number of reflective materials [29] and
consequently, influence on learning attainment [93] and at the same time the ambient noise in a classroom might be increased [31,32].
Fig. 8 presents acoustic parameters evaluated for each material design enabler according to references from the review session.
Using the right materials for the floor might change the acoustic quality of a classroom. A study by Ref. [94] found that renovated
classrooms using higher absorptive materials managed to reduce reverberation time by up to 30 %. According to simulation works
from Ref. [54], adding 50 % absorptive materials at both sides of the classroom wall, employing carpet for floors and gypsum for the
ceiling result in preferable reverberation time, D50 and STI. The floor area covered with carpet showed less noise intensity due to the
sound absorbed by the carpet [95]. However, some countries do not permit the use of carpet as floor covering due to hygiene regu-
lations [96]. It has been observed that due to quieter conditions created by having adequate absorption on room surfaces, signal to
noise ratio was also increased, which is significant to speech intelligibility quality [43], reduced the sound pressure level up to 5 dB,
sound clarity increased by 20 % [44] and can be evenly distributed throughout the classrooms [97]. Building material selection
certainly greatly impacts the reduction of noise within the learning spaces [98]. According to Ref. [45], unsuitable materials employed
in a classroom in Kerala contribute to the excessive ambient noise and high RT value. Based on [46], installing a new suspended ceiling,
single-glazing window, and a window curtain improved the ambient noise problem in the classroom.
Proper configurations of materials used in a classroom must be well indicated. Materials with higher absorption coefficients are
necessarily placed on the floor, wall, and ceiling to comply with standard reverberation time for classrooms [33,34,49,96,99]. Studies
performed by Refs. [36–38,52] revealed the installation of materials with higher absorption coefficients on ceiling surfaces improved
the reverberation time and STI of the classroom. In addition, the presence of new plasterboard [50] and gypsum board [51] as ceiling
finishes improved the reverberation time and speech intelligibility of the classrooms [53]. The usage of absorptive materials [41,42] as
well as mineral wools [26] and green materials [13,40] at the rear wall in a classroom showed a decrease in reverberation time value
and significant improvement of STI in both occupied and unoccupied classrooms conditions.
Installation of ceiling finishes with reflective properties at the speaker position facilitates the sound to travel towards the end of the
classrooms. At the same time, absorptive materials are more suitable to be placed at the rear/back wall and ceiling to reduce multiple
reflections [25]. Mir and Abdou [56] proposed the best configuration for the ceiling was 50 % absorptive materials at the perimeter
and 10 % reflective material at the central location. For the wall configurations, the best design was to place reflective materials at the
lower part of the wall area and absorptive materials from the middle to the upper part of the walls to achieve the ideal results for RT,
STI, and C50. Also, the configuration of absorbers must be in the middle of the ceiling, walls, and floor to create better classroom
acoustic performance [47]. On the other hand [57], stated that speech intelligibility in a classroom can be maximised when absorptive
materials are placed on both sides of the walls and non-uniformly installed at the rear part of the ceiling and wall. The design and

In addition to using absorbers in a classroom, another alternative for acoustic treatment is installing an adequate diffuser at the
right location. Using absorbers alone reduces reverberation time and increases the early to late-arriving sound ratio (C50). The
drawback of this would be the sound strength being reduced to a certain level, affecting the listeners sitting at the rear of the classroom.
It was found that using a combined diffuser and absorber in a classroom enhanced the important acoustic parameters: RT, G and C50
[7,57]. Furthermore, listeners sitting at the rear of the classroom can benefit more if diffusers were installed at the lower part of the
front wall [48] and absorptive materials at the ceiling significantly reduced the reverberation time of a classroom [55]. Classrooms
with excessive absorptive materials are not recommended, as they may create a dead environment. Combining absorptive, reflective,
and diffusive materials is much appreciated to control the sound propagation and reverberation properties in a specific space.
In summary, the two primary factors associated with surface materials are the material types and the arrangements of the materials.
The acoustic performance in classrooms was considerably enhanced by carefully choosing appropriate surface materials, such as
absorbers, diffusers, and reflectors and by determining the amount and placement of these materials. Ensuring optimal speech
intelligibility in the classroom requires careful consideration of material selection and arrangement, focusing on meeting ideal pref-
erences for significant acoustic parameters.
3.4.2. Volume
Reverberation time in an enclosed space is greatly influenced by room volume, where the greater the room volume, the longer the
reverberation time in the room [100]. As stated in Ref. [101], using reverberation time as a room evaluation tool is a promising
strategy to develop better acoustic conditions for speech. In the three analytical approaches, Sabine, Norris-Eryington, and
Mellington-Sette, room volume plays an important role in determining the nature of reverberation time, as shown in equations (1)–(3).

A classroom with a huge volume and without acoustic treatment may have a poor acoustic environment. Lim et al. [52] discovered a
classroom with a high ceiling height that displayed bad reverberation conditions. However, as the volume of the room was reduced by
lowering the ceiling height, reverberation time and STI can be improved [60].
In contrast, according to Leccese et al. [35], room volume is not the main concern in achieving the best acoustic condition.
Regardless of the classroom volume, if an acceptable number of absorptive materials were installed, crucial parameters such as
reverberation time and STI would likely be improved. Moreover, various equations to predict STI based on RT can be performed
without considering the volume of the room. Nevertheless, the influence of volume as a fundamental attribute in determining the
reverberation time should not be neglected. It was recommended that suitable reverberation time depends on the room volume, as
displayed in various formulas [102]. The reverberation time recommendation for various room activities based on different room
volume sizes had been stated by Long [103].

3.4.3. Noise
Excessive ambient noise levels were a major concern, as was improper room acoustic quality [21]. The background noise in a
classroom mostly originates from the sound produced by outdoor activities, learning activities in a classroom, and indoor and outdoor
electrical appliances. Excessive noise in a classroom significantly affects acoustic comfort, listeners’ comprehension, and speakers’
well-being. A guideline by Berglund et al. [104] stated that the recommended noise levels for unoccupied and occupied classrooms are
35 and 55 dB, respectively. It is essential to ensure the unoccupied noise level does not exceed 35 dB as recommended by ANSI S12.60,
even though the noise level will increase upon classroom occupation [105]. Excessive noise in a classroom affects the teaching and
learning process and creates bad acoustic conditions [106]. Based on research initiated by Gramez and Boubenider [28], a seminar
room located next to a machinery room was severely affected by the noise produced by the machine.
Indoor noise sources produced by ventilation systems require attention as well. Hodgson et al. [63] found that the noise level
obtained from field measurements in unoccupied and occupied classrooms was 39–42 dB and 40–45 dB, respectively. The value
indicated that the noise from the ventilation system affected the classroom’s acoustic environment [64]. When a ventilation system is
turned on, the noise produced by the ventilation system reduces both STI and SNR values in classrooms [69]. Another prominent
source of indoor noise reported was students’ activity in classrooms [61]. A study to determine the classroom noise level in various
schools in Malaysia was performed by Ismail et al. [62]. The study discovered that all classrooms exhibited excessive noise levels
ranging from 63.21 to 75.71 dB. From the investigation, improper classroom materials were used, contributing to the unreasonable
noise level. A similar investigation to determine noise level and speech level during lectures in 11 universities was conducted by Choi
[73,78]. The study reported that the average noise level during the lecture was 44.3 dB, and the mean speech level was 51.5 dB, which
generated SNR values of 7.2 dB. Excessive noise levels from students inside the classroom made it difficult for the teachers to increase
their vocal effort and risked their health conditions [65]. This statement is also supported by Silva et al. [66] and Ramma [67], where
noise from students in a classroom is more crucial than outdoor noise and eventually affects the overall learning process and activities.
Students’ learning process deteriorates in a noisy classroom. When the background noise level exceeds the speaker’s speech level
(low signal-to-noise ratio), students will encounter listening problems, which eventually reduces their comprehension. Peng and Wu
[68] and Peng et al. [75] found that speech intelligibility results among Chinese students were improved as SNR increased, and
performance was downgraded when the SNR value decreased. Besides, classroom noise from mechanical and electrical appliances (i.e.,
air conditioning system, lighting, and LCD projector) affected students’ comprehension test results. Longoni et al. [69] stated that the
noise spectrum produced by the heating, ventilation, and air conditioning (HVAC) system greatly influences speech intelligibility
across a wide frequency range in an enclosed room. As the noise level increased, students’ comprehension ability was reduced [70],
and they became more anxious [13]. Similar findings stated significant negative correlations between noise level and reading
comprehension among students in the United States of America [71,72]. In research on speech intelligibility tests for adult students
conducted at a University in Korea, the findings show that adult listeners managed to get a 95 % score for the intelligibility test with an
SNR value of 3 dB [107]. This indicates that young adult students did not encounter difficulties comprehending the speech in a lower
SNR condition.
Classroom noise is crucial for creating an acoustically comfortable environment that promotes effective teaching and learning. To
create an optimal learning environment that promotes students’ academic performance and well-being, it is necessary to limit the
indoor noise generated by mechanical ventilation and student activities, as well as outdoor noise, to a specific maximum level. In

3.4.4. Occupancy
The acoustic quality of a classroom is also influenced by the level of occupancy. Various studies have been conducted to determine
the effects of occupants on classroom acoustic quality. The presence of occupants in a specific space is anticipated to absorb more
reflected sound and thus reduce the reverberation time. It was found that the absorption coefficient of a single occupant in reflective
classrooms is roughly 0.6 m2/person and 0.4 m2/person for absorptive classrooms [108]. Based on Dlhý and Zrnekova´ [79], rever-
beration time in an unoccupied classroom could be decreased by 33 % (from 1.44s to 0.95s) when the classroom was 100 % occupied.
Significant improvement in reverberation time can be achieved only in reflective classrooms. As described in Ref. [77], a small
increment in overall sound absorption was noticed in a fully occupied absorptive classroom. However, significant reverberation time
improvement from 1.38 s to 0.72 s was recorded when the reflective classrooms were added with 50 % occupancy.
Furthermore, it was also found that a number of occupancies greatly impacted large classrooms with high reflective properties
[109]. When occupants were added, approximately 44 % of reverberation was reduced in a large nonabsorbent classroom. In research
done by Choi [108], the effects of occupants on acoustic parameters varied according to occupants’ distribution percentage. As for
reflective classrooms’ reverberation time was reduced from 1.63 s to 0.75 s when the classroom is 100 % occupied. However, there was
little impact on reverberation time for absorptive classrooms where the reverberation time value was 0.22 s and decreased to 0.19 s
from unoccupied to 100 % occupancy.
Nevertheless, it must be noted that classroom acoustic design is impossible to generalise solely based on the number of occupants.
Acoustic parameters for classrooms vary according to the age of the occupants. Peng and Wu [68] believed that younger children
required higher SNR and lower RT when compared to adults. For higher-grade children, the requirements for SNR and RT were
broader. To achieve 95 % scores on speech intelligibility test, younger age groups required higher STI values than adults [80]. This is
due to the different students’ ages that might influence their ability to perceive the information the teacher gave as the brain is still
developing until adulthood.
Therefore, it is crucial to consider the occupancy of a classroom during the design phase since it significantly impacts classroom
acoustic quality. Occupied classroom design criteria must be considered to fill the void, and a holistic approach must be further
scrutinised. The acoustic performance in a classroom is influenced by both the number of occupants and the ages of the listeners.
Listeners’ age necessitates distinct hearing preferences based on individual characteristics. Therefore, the classroom design ought to
consider the characteristics of the individuals present to satisfy their specific preferences for sound quality. Table A.3 (see Appendix 1)
provides a concise overview of the references included in the review activity.
3.4.5. Sound amplification system
A good listening environment in a classroom is necessary to help students improve their attention and comprehension ability. Noisy
classroom conditions impact the effectiveness of speech intelligibility when the background noise is greater than the speech level.
Hence, the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) must be considered as it greatly affects students and teachers. Using a sound amplification
system in an acceptable acoustic comfort classroom achieved +13 dB SNR [84]. In a different study, with a sound amplification system
in a classroom, the teacher’s speech level and SNR were increased by 8.62 dB and 4.92 dB, correspondingly [82]. A finding from
Sundaravadhanan et al. [49] revealed that teachers had to raise their voices during lessons due to insufficient SNR for a hearing
distance of 2 m. A sound amplification system was recommended to overcome this issue as it improved student and teacher
communication and academic performance [110,111]. The effectiveness of the sound amplification system used in a classroom de-
pends on the type and configuration. A new appropriate sound amplification system replacement using line arrays and filler config-
uration had increased speech level, and more diffused sound fields were attained during active lessons [43].
However, using sound amplification systems in a classroom has some limitations and drawbacks. A sound amplification system can
be effective and possible only for fully enclosed classrooms to avoid the spillover effect [49]. For classrooms with open windows and
doors, unwanted noise from high speech levels can be transmitted effortlessly to adjacent classrooms [82]. Hence, adopting sound
amplification equipment in classrooms is vital for ensuring adequate and uniform sound dispersion to the audience across the
educational space. Due to high noise levels in classrooms that do not meet required standards, it is necessary to incorporate sound
amplification equipment to achieve the desired signal-to-noise ratio (SNR). Table A.4 (see Appendix 1) briefly overviews the general
data gathered from the referred references.
3.4.6. Layout
Classrooms with different layout arrangements lead to different acoustic performances. The most commonly used classroom lay-
outs are enclosed, semi-open, and open-plan. As stated by Mealings et al. [85,86], the reverberation times of enclosed and open-plan
classrooms were slightly different. The findings showed that reverberation time for an enclosed space classroom was 0.5 s, while
open-plan classroom increased up to 0.7 s. The results showed that classroom layout influenced the classroom acoustic comfort, and it
was found that different layouts require different acoustic conditions [112]. Apart from that, the SNR value recorded for open-plan
classrooms ranged from +0.8–6.1 dB, while the enclosed classrooms recorded an SNR value of +12.7 dB during the noisy work ac-
tivities [86]. It was found that open-plan classrooms are not recommended for speech communication as the intrusive noise was high
compared to enclosed classrooms as it may affect the students’ speech perception, especially for listening activities [113].
Classroom acoustic comfort is also influenced by seating layout arrangement. A study to investigate classroom acoustic perfor-
mance based on seating arrangement was conducted by Lim et al. [52]. The findings showed that classrooms with modular

3.5. Proposed classroom acoustic comfort conceptual framework
Synthesised findings from previous research have been conducted, particularly on the comfort of classroom acoustics. All reviewed
articles discussed prominent design enablers that influenced the overall perception of classroom acoustic performance. According to
the reviewed findings, the most crucial enabler that constitutes acoustic comfort in the classroom is the application of finished ma-
terials. Types and configurations of materials used in an enclosed classroom determine the acoustic conditions for a better hearing
environment. The noise disruption experienced by the listeners in a classroom degrades the acoustic comfort. The presence of noise in a
classroom is mostly produced by nearby traffic, mechanical and electrical equipment (i.e., the air conditioning system, lighting, etc.),
and students’ activity in the classroom. Excessive noise levels influence students’ ability to comprehend speech and affect attention
levels during the learning session. Aside from that, classroom layout, which includes seating arrangement, layout design, and student-
teacher distance, influences a classroom’s acoustic performance. Other enablers, such as volume, occupancy, and the amplification
system, also impact the classroom acoustic environment. Only five acoustic parameters from the initial parameter numbers were
included in the conceptual framework. The reduction of acoustic parameters is due to the limited number of studies and insignificant
impact observed. A proposed conceptual framework of the plausible design enablers that determine the comfort of classroom acoustics
to achieve acceptable performance is presented in Fig. 9.
4. Conclusion
A conceptual framework of design enablers for achieving acoustic comfort in classrooms was developed through the systematic
review of 74 articles. The detailed review of the current literature is motivated by the increasing interest in acquiring optimal acoustic
comfort for the purpose of teaching and learning. The interest in this subject arises from the extensive accounts of occupants facing
significant academic challenges, which are attributed to inadequate acoustic conditions in classrooms. Although there is a clear un-
derstanding of the components that contribute to conducive classroom acoustics, effectively evaluating and synthesising the rela-
tionship between each design enabler and specific acoustic parameters requires substantial dedication. By directly addressing the
research questions (RQ), this conclusion provides a clear and concise summary of the study’s findings.
RQ1 - What design enablers must be considered in ensuring the acoustical performance of a classroom? The results indicate that the level
of acoustic comfort in the classroom is categorised by three key attributes: physical, human, and noise. Firstly, the physical attributes
encompass four design enablers: material, volume, arrangement, and amplification. Secondly, the human attributes consider age and
the number of occupants, as they can substantially affect the acoustic comfort of the classroom. The diverse age range of the audience
requires distinct acoustic preferences, and the acoustic performance is also influenced by the number of people in the classroom.
Thirdly, the main contributors to noise levels significantly affecting classroom acoustic comfort are the HVAC system, students’ ac-
tivities, and environmental elements. Despite the different characteristics of noise, both indoor and outdoor noises can be considered a
single design enabler that may have an impact on classroom acoustic comfort. These undesirable sounds will impair occupants’
auditory acuity and hinder their ability to understand and comprehend speech.
RQ2 - How do the acoustic parameters respond to different design enablers in a classroom? The findings underscore the importance of
various acoustic parameters in the design of classroom comfort. Several design enablers extensively influence these parameters. For
instance, the reverberation time (RT) condition in classrooms is notably impacted by surface materials and ceiling height while
remaining largely unaffected by other design enablers. Conversely, speech transmission index (STI) results primarily depend on noise
levels, layout, and amplification system, indicating that specific design enablers distinctly affect these parameters, requiring attentive
consideration. In addition, the findings indicate that both the classroom layout (hearing distance) and the material enabler influence
the clarity of speech. The study indicates that identical design enabler has a substantial impact on the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR). The
SNR results are influenced by other enablers, specifically noise, amplification systems, and occupancy. Therefore, it demonstrates that
each design enabler has a distinct influence on the particular acoustic parameter of the classroom.
The study’s findings contribute to the current knowledge by providing an in-depth analysis of the design enablers and their in-
fluence on the parameters that indicate acoustic comfort in a classroom. The proposed conceptual framework can serve as an
